title: Part A: Where Uploads Go
statement: A recipe app receives about 100,000 photos a day, 2 MB each, up to 50 per second at peak. Its app servers can carry about 1 GB per second in total. Its database must stay under 500 GB so that nightly backups finish. Object storage with signed upload URLs is available. Exercise assumptions: only logged-in users may upload, into their own recipes; the team prefers that photo bytes do not pass through the app servers. Which upload path fits?
examples: Bytes per day = photos a day × size.
constraints: Stay within the app servers' 1 GB per second.
Prefer keeping photo bytes off the app servers.

approaches.name: The app checks rights and returns a signed upload URL; the phone sends the photo straight to object storage; the app saves the details and key
approaches.hint: Check on the server, bytes go straight to storage
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: One small request to the app per upload
approaches.space: 200 GB a day in object storage; a few hundred bytes per photo in the database
approaches.why: Storage takes the 100,000 × 2 MB = 200 GB a day; the database grows by only the details. No photo bytes cross the app servers.

approaches.name: The phone sends the photo to the app server, which writes it to object storage
approaches.label: valid
approaches.time: 50 × 2 MB = 100 MB per second through the app servers at peak
approaches.space: The same as the direct path
approaches.why: The database stays small and 100 MB per second fits within 1 GB per second, but every byte passes through the app servers, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: Store each photo's bytes in a database column
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.time: 100 MB per second into the database at peak
approaches.space: 200 GB a day in the database
approaches.why: At 200 GB a day the database passes 500 GB within three days, and backups stop finishing.

title: Part B: Searching Messages
statement: A team chat app keeps 20 million messages, about 100 bytes each, in its database. Users search about 100 times per second, by one or more words. Exercise assumptions: results must come back within 300 ms; a new message must be findable within 1 minute; the team prefers new messages to be findable as soon as possible; a separate search index can be fed by the database's change events or rebuilt in batches.
examples: Reading every message is 20 million × 100 bytes = 2 GB per search.

approaches.name: An inverted index of tokenized words, updated from each new message's change event within seconds
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: A few sorted lists per search, milliseconds
approaches.space: One list entry per word per message
approaches.why: Each search reads only the lists for its words, far within 300 ms, and a new message is in the index within seconds.

approaches.name: The same inverted index, updated every 30 seconds in a batch
approaches.hint: Word → message IDs, refreshed in batches
approaches.label: valid
approaches.space: One list entry per word per message
approaches.why: Searches are just as fast, and new messages appear within 30 seconds, inside the 1-minute limit, but later than with change events, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: WHERE text LIKE '%word%' on the messages table
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Every search reads all 2 GB of messages; at 100 searches per second that is 200 GB of reading per second, so results cannot come back within 300 ms.

title: Part C: IDs Made on Phones
statement: A notes app lets about 5 million users create notes on their phones while offline; notes are sent to the server later. Exercise assumptions: a note's ID is chosen on the phone when the note is created, with no server reachable; IDs must never clash across all phones; there is no way to give each phone a unique machine number; the team prefers IDs that sort by creation time so lists can show the newest first.
examples: A UUID version 7 starts with 48 bits of milliseconds, followed by random bits.
constraints: IDs are made on the phone while offline.
Prefer IDs that sort by creation time.

approaches.name: A UUID version 7: the time in milliseconds followed by random bits
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Phones need no server and no machine number; the random bits make a clash between phones practically impossible, and IDs sort by creation time.

approaches.name: A random UUID (version 4)
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: It works offline and practically never clashes, but the IDs do not sort by time, so lists need a separate time column to show the newest first, against the stated preference.

approaches.name: An auto-increment number from the server's database
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The phone is offline when the note is created, so it cannot get the next number; numbering on each phone would clash across phones.
